what_it_does: Sequence alignment is the process of finding where two strings of letters (DNA, protein amino acids, or plain text) match, with allowances for insertions, deletions, and substitutions — a fundamental operation in genomics and bioinformatics. Prior dedicated chips were built for one specific flavor of alignment and fell apart when asked to handle different scoring rules, gap penalties, or alphabet types. At the same time, general-purpose CPUs and GPUs handle any alignment problem but waste energy doing so. SMX combines both worlds with two pieces: a set of new processor instructions (extensions to the CPU's language) that handle the irregular edge cases of alignment quickly, and a separate small coprocessor tile — a grid of simple arithmetic units arranged to process the dynamic programming table in a diagonal wave-front pattern — for the repetitive inner loop. The combined design handles DNA, protein, and text alignment under varied scoring rules, fits in roughly a third of the area of a small CPU core, and was verified in a 22-nanometer chip process.
